summary: Ethiopia lies in the Horn of Africa and is one of the oldest independent countries in Africa; apart from a brief Italian occupation it was never colonized, and it is also the seat of the African Union headquarters.

ranking.name: Ethiopian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In the 4th century King Ezana of Aksum, under the influence of the Syrian missionary Frumentius, converted to Christianity, making Ethiopia one of the world’s earliest Christian countries; in the 5th–6th centuries the “Nine Saints” spread the faith further into the countryside, and in the 12th–13th centuries the Lalibela kings built the famous complex of rock-hewn churches. Orthodoxy was long the state religion, closely tied to the myth of royal descent, and church and state were separated only when the Derg military junta overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974. Believers are concentrated in the Amhara and Tigray regions of the northern highlands.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Around 615, followers of the Prophet Muhammad crossed the sea to seek refuge with the king of Aksum and were given protection, so Islam regards Ethiopia as a friendly land. Later, through Red Sea and Gulf of Aden trade, Islam spread in the east and south, and Harar became an important Islamic city; in the 16th century Ahmad Gran of the Adal Sultanate waged a war that nearly conquered the entire highlands. Today’s Muslims are mainly Oromo, Somali and Afar, distributed in the east and southeast.

ranking.name: Protestantism (P’ent’ay)
ranking.description: In the 19th and 20th centuries Protestant missions from Sweden, the United States and Germany preached in the south and west, and the Mekane Yesus Church, founded in 1959, became the largest Protestant church. From 1974 to 1991 the Derg regime suppressed churches, but after 1991 religious freedom allowed Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity to grow explosively among the Oromo and the peoples of the south, rising from a single-digit percentage in the 1980s to nearly two-tenths; Prime Minister Abiy, who took office in 2018, is also a Pentecostal.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs include the Oromo “Waaqeffanna,” which worships the sky god Waaq, and the “Irreecha” thanksgiving festival at the end of each rainy season still draws millions of participants; the peoples of the southern Omo Valley also preserve ancestor and nature worship. These beliefs have long been squeezed by Orthodoxy and Islam, and the share of followers is not high.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the early 17th century Portuguese Jesuits led Emperor Susenyos to convert to Catholicism in 1622, but this provoked a civil war, and after he abdicated in 1632 the Jesuits were expelled. From the 19th century the Catholic Church resumed missionary work in the south and in the Eritrean region, and expanded during the Italian occupation of 1936–1941, but believers have always been few.

religion.background: Ethiopia is one of Africa’s oldest Christian countries; the Kingdom of Aksum converted to Christianity in the 4th century, and Orthodoxy long served as the state religion and shaped national culture; Islam also arrived very early, in the 7th century, taking root in the east and lowlands and creating a long coexistence of the two major religions. The wars of the Adal Sultanate in the 16th century and the Jesuits’ conversion attempt in the 17th century both shook the position of Orthodoxy. After the monarchy was overthrown in 1974 religion no longer had state support, and after 1991 Pentecostal Protestantism grew rapidly and became the third-largest religion.

language.official: The federal working language is Amharic; since 2020 Oromo, Tigrinya, Somali and Afar have also been added as federal working languages.

ranking.name: Oromo
ranking.description: Oromo belongs to the Cushitic family and is the most widely spoken ethnic language in Ethiopia. The Oromo expanded and migrated northward in large numbers in the 16th century and spread across vast areas of the center and south. During the imperial era the government promoted Amharic, and Oromo was banned from publication and education; in 1991 it adopted the Latin-based “Qubee” script and became the official language of Oromia Region, and in 2020 the federal government also made it a working language.

ranking.name: Amharic
ranking.description: Amharic belongs to the Semitic family and is written in the Ge‘ez script. After the restoration of the Solomonic dynasty in 1270 it became the court language, and the southward expansion of Menelik II in the late 19th century and the centralizing policies of Haile Selassie in the 20th century made it the language of administration and education across the country. Today it is the federal working language and a lingua franca among peoples, the main language of the capital Addis Ababa, with native speakers concentrated in the Amhara Region.

ranking.name: Somali
ranking.description: Somali is spoken in the Somali Region (the Ogaden) in the southeast, which Menelik II incorporated into his domain in the late 19th century, and in 1977–1978 Somalia launched the Ogaden War to contest the area. After federalism was implemented in 1991, Somali became the official language of the Somali Region.

ranking.name: Tigrinya
ranking.description: Tigrinya is spoken in the northern Tigray Region and derives from the Ge‘ez cultural area of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum. In 1991 a party with the Tigrayans at its core led the overthrow of the Derg regime, and Tigrinya for a time gained greatly in political influence; the Tigray War of 2020–2022 then caused enormous devastation to local society.

language.history: Ethiopia has more than eighty languages, belonging to the Semitic, Cushitic, Omotic and Nilo-Saharan families. The ancient Kingdom of Aksum used Ge‘ez and developed the distinctive Ge‘ez script; Ge‘ez later became the liturgical language of Orthodoxy, while Amharic and Tigrinya developed from the same tradition. From the Middle Ages Amharic became the court language, and in the 20th century the imperial government used it to promote national unity while suppressing other ethnic languages. After 1991 an ethnically based federalism was implemented, each region can use its own language, and the status of languages such as Oromo has risen greatly.

ranking.name: Injera
ranking.description: Teff flour is fermented with water for several days and then cooked on a large flat pan into a thin pancake half a meter in diameter, covered in small holes, with a slightly sour taste.
ranking.history: Teff is a grain native to the Ethiopian highlands, cultivated here for thousands of years, drought-tolerant and adapted to the highland climate, and was already an important staple in the era of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum. Injera is both plate and utensil, as people tear off a piece with the right hand and wrap stew to put in the mouth, and a family or guests sharing one large plate symbolizes unity and trust. The “gursha,” in which the host feeds a guest a mouthful by hand, is a courtesy expressing respect and intimacy, and injera is therefore regarded as the core of Ethiopian culture.

ranking.name: Doro wat (spicy chicken stew)
ranking.description: Plenty of onion is slow-cooked for a long time, then berbere chili spice, spiced butter (niter kibbeh) and chicken are added and stewed, and hard-boiled eggs are put in at the end.
ranking.history: Doro wat is regarded by many Ethiopians as the national dish, and it is very laborious to make, as the onions alone take hours to cook. It is most closely tied to Orthodox festivals: after the Lenten fast of more than fifty days before Easter ends, people break the fast with doro wat at Easter (Fasika), and it is also sure to be served at Christmas (Genna) and the September New Year. The chili in berbere is native to the Americas and arrived by trade only in about the 16th–17th centuries, and combined with local spices formed today’s flavor.

ranking.name: Kitfo (minced raw beef)
ranking.description: Lean raw beef is chopped finely and mixed with mitmita chili spice powder and clarified spiced butter, eaten raw or lightly warmed, with cheese and injera.
ranking.history: Kitfo originated with the Gurage people of south-central Ethiopia, where it is an important dish for entertaining honored guests and celebrating festivals, often served with “kocho” flatbread made from false banana (ensete). The Gurage especially prepare large amounts of kitfo at the Meskel festival each September. As Gurage merchants moved to the major cities, it became a popular restaurant dish across the country in the 20th century, and Addis Ababa has many specialty shops.

ranking.name: Shiro (chickpea stew)
ranking.description: Roasted chickpea or fava bean flour is cooked with onion, garlic and berbere spice, with water or oil, into a creamy, paste-like stew.
ranking.history: Ethiopian Orthodox believers fast on Wednesdays and Fridays every week and during Lent, abstaining from meat, eggs and dairy, with more than one hundred eighty fasting days a year, so a rich vegetarian cuisine has developed, and shiro is the most common dish among them. Its ingredients are cheap and it cooks quickly, so regardless of religion it is an everyday home dish. During fasting periods, restaurants offer platters of many vegetarian stews (beyaynetu), and shiro always sits in the center.

ranking.name: Tibs
ranking.description: Beef or lamb is cut into pieces and quickly stir-fried with onion, chili, rosemary and spiced butter, tender and fragrant, and is often served hot in a clay dish.
ranking.history: Tibs is a dish Ethiopians prepare for celebrations and for entertaining guests; after the long fasting periods end, or at festivals, weddings and when welcoming visitors from afar, people buy meat or slaughter a sheep to make tibs to share. In the capital many butcher shops also operate as restaurants, where customers choose the meat and have it stir-fried on the spot, forming a distinctive food culture. It is also the most common introductory dish when entertaining foreign guests.
